name: Azelaic acid scalp
lead: Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used topically at 15 to 20 percent for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation.[1] In hair-loss communities it is applied to the scalp or included in compounded anti-hair-loss lotions with the aim of slowing thinning and keeping hair density, because of claims that it mildly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme targeted by finasteride and dutasteride.[3][4]

Wikipedia cites a 1988 in vitro report in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate strongly inhibited 5-alpha-reductase in human skin; the article notes this is a single in vitro study and not clinical evidence that topical azelaic acid alone has this effect in vivo.[1] A forum poster in 2000 asked about a French study combining zinc, vitamin B6 and azelaic acid reported to lower scalp DHT, showing how the idea circulated early.[5]

A small early phase 1 trial of azelaic acid in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a scarring alopecia, is registered.[2] Lifting forums mention azelaic acid in compounded topical mixes with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride, usually discussed by people also dealing with hair thinning from anabolic use.[3][6]
infobox: Wheat, rye, barley; produced by Malassezia furfur[1]

paras: Topical azelaic acid treats mild to moderate acne, papulopustular rosacea, melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[1]

Users discuss scalp application as a mild anti-androgen add-on. One T Nation poster suggests having a compounding pharmacy mix 10% minoxidil, tretinoin, azelaic acid, 0.1% finasteride, biotin and hydrocortisone into a single lotion, and another asks whether topical azelaic acid cream can control scalp DHT and whether it is safe for someone on testosterone therapy.[3][4] No approved hair-loss indication exists for azelaic acid.

Reported actions include bacteriostatic activity, normalising follicular keratinisation, reducing reactive oxygen species and cytokines, and tyrosinase inhibition.[1] The 5-alpha-reductase claim rests on the 1988 in vitro combination study.[1]
Skin dryness and irritation are the main reported effects, particularly in people with eczema.[1]

sections.h: Use in hair-loss and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, azelaic acid comes up in threads about hair loss during testosterone therapy or anabolic cycles, where members list it among options beyond the 'big 3' of finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole shampoo, and a 2016 T Nation article on hair loss summarises treatments.[6][7] Members also share a recalled report of a zinc, B6 and azelaic acid combination.[5] These are personal and secondhand accounts.

A registered early phase 1 trial (NCT05416333) is testing azelaic acid in CCCA in 18 participants; it began in 2024 and is listed as active, not recruiting, and no results were loaded for this article.[2] No studies found of azelaic acid for androgenetic alopecia in the sources used.

timeline.event: In vitro report of azelaic acid plus zinc sulfate inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase.[1]

lore.intro: Azelaic acid appears in T Nation hair-loss threads and compounded-topical suggestions as a mild 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid on the scalp acts as a mild 5-ARI and lowers scalp DHT.
claims.believers: Posters cite a French study said to lower scalp DHT with zinc, B6 and azelaic acid and say they have heard it can control scalp DHT.[4][5]
claims.experts: The cited inhibition was an in vitro finding with zinc sulfate; no clinical evidence of this effect from topical use alone is described.[1]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid can be combined with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride in a compounded lotion.
claims.believers: One T Nation member recommends a compounding pharmacy mix that includes azelaic acid alongside other actives.[3]
claims.experts: No published trial of such a mixture including azelaic acid for pattern hair loss was found; its registered scalp trial concerns CCCA.[2]

card.summary: Acne/rosacea acid with a lab-only 5-ARI claim, used in hair stacks without scalp trials for pattern hair loss.

quick.overview:
Azelaic acid is a skin treatment for acne and rosacea. Some hair-loss users put it on the scalp for a claimed mild finasteride-like effect.

The claim comes from a 1988 lab study; no pattern-hair-loss trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It reduces bacteria, inflammation and pigment production; 5-alpha-reductase inhibition was shown in vitro in combination with zinc sulfate.
quick.risks: Dryness and irritation are the main reported effects.

chain: Applied to scalp, often within a compounded topical
Proposed mild local 5-alpha-reductase inhibition, lowering scalp DHT
Slower thinning and better hair density, claimed rather than shown
angle.text: Hair-loss forum members add azelaic acid to scalp stacks hoping for a mild anti-DHT effect that helps preserve hair. The supporting data cited are a 1988 laboratory result; scalp trials in pattern hair loss have not been published.
